Not “I can cd ” — fluency means you can answer “where did that output go?”, “why can’t this process read that file?”, and “what will this command do to the other eleven files matching the glob?” before you run it. EX200 begins with an essential tools domain that is deceptively small: redirection, grep , regex, SSH, archives, links, permissions, documentation. Those objectives are worth roughly a fifth of the exam, and they are the ones people lose points on because they stopped thinking about them years ago. Streams: the plumbing you cannot skip A process gets three file descriptors. Standard input (0) is what it reads, standard output (1) is what it prints, standard error (2) is where it complains. Redirection is just reassigning descriptors, and the shell applies it before the command runs. streams.sh shell copy # Send stdout to a file, truncating it $ ls -l /etc > /tmp/etc.txt # Append instead of truncate $ ls -l /var/log >> /tmp/etc.txt # Capture BOTH streams into one file (order matters) $ dnf install httpd > /tmp/install.log 2>&1 # Discard noise, keep the signal $ find / -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null | wc -l # Feed a file as stdin $ sort < /etc/passwd # Here-document: multi-line stdin inside a script $ cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/motd Welcome to rhel.lab.example.com Authorised use only. EOF The classic order mistake 2>&1 > file and > file 2>&1 are not the same. In the first, stderr is pointed at the terminal (stdout’s current target) and then stdout is moved to the file, so errors still hit your screen. In the second, stdout goes to the file first and stderr is then duplicated onto it. Only the second captures both. Redirections are evaluated left to right, like assignments. Text surgery: grep, cut, sed, awk You do not need to be a regex wizard to pass. You need four tools and the confidence to combine them. Daily text tools Command Does Real invocation grep -Ei Line filter; -E extended regex, -i ignore case, -r recursive, -n line numbers, -v invert grep -Ein '^PermitRootLogin' /etc/ssh/sshd_config sed -i Stream edit in place; s/old/new/g sed -i 's/^SELINUX=.*/SELINUX=enforcing/' /etc/selinux/config awk Field-aware processing; default separator is whitespace, -F: for passwd awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd cut Column extraction by delimiter cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd sort | uniq -c | sort -rn The frequency pipeline: count repeats, biggest first awk '{print $1}' /var/log/secure | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head regex-cheatsheet BRE / ERE copy # Anchors and classes — the 90% you actually use ^ start of line $ end of line . any single character .* any run of characters (greedy) [abc] one of a, b, c [^abc] anything except [a-z0-9] ranges \b word boundary (GNU) \{2,4\} repeat count in BRE; {2,4} in ERE with -E ( | ) alternation in ERE only # Find every commented or uncommented sshd setting that is not the default $ grep -E '^[[:space:]]*#?[[:space:]]*PasswordAuthentication' /etc/ssh/sshd_config Permissions: the model, then the syntax Mode bits are an octal triplet per class: owner, group, others. rwx is 4+2+1, so 750 means owner rwx, group r-x, others nothing. Two extra concepts decide most exam tasks: umask (default mode is 666 & ~umask for files, 777 & ~umask for directories) and the special bits . Special bits that appear in real incident reports Bit Octal Effect Legitimate use setuid 4000 Runs with the file owner’s UID passwd , su , mount — root-owned, tiny, audited setgid 2000 File: runs with group. Directory: new files inherit the directory’s group Shared team directories — the correct fix for “my colleague can’t edit it” sticky 1000 Only the owner may delete their file in a shared directory /tmp , /var/tmp permissions.sh shell copy # Symbolic and octal are equally valid on the exam # chmod u=rw,g=r,o= /etc/motd # chmod 640 /etc/motd # Recursive ownership, then verify # chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html # ls -ld /var/www/html # Shared directory: setgid + sticky, group-writable, no world access # mkdir -p /srv/shared # chgrp devs /srv/shared # chmod 2770 /srv/shared # Find everything world-writable outside volatile dirs — an audit staple # find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 ! -path '/tmp/*' ! -path '/var/tmp/*' -ls 2>/dev/null # Find SUID binaries (an attacker's shopping list) # find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -exec ls -l {} \; 2>/dev/null Bad decision #3 — chmod -R 777 to “fix” a permission problem It works, in the same way that removing the front door fixes a broken lock. World-writable web content lets any local user — including a compromised service account — replace your PHP or your static assets, and it usually breaks SELinux expectations at the same time. It also hides the real cause, which is almost always one of: wrong owner, wrong group, missing traverse ( x ) permission on a parent directory, or a bad umask. Diagnose with namei -l /var/www/html/index.php , which prints the effective permissions of every path component. Then fix the one that is wrong. Links: two different objects A hard link is a second name for the same inode. It cannot cross filesystems and cannot point at a directory. A soft (symbolic) link is a tiny file containing a path; it can cross filesystems, can dangle, and can point at directories — which is why every service configuration in /etc that “just points somewhere” is a symlink. links.sh shell copy # ln /etc/hosts /root/hosts-hard # same inode, survives deleting the original name # ln -s /opt/app/current/release.conf /etc/app.conf # Prove the difference $ stat -c '%i %h %n' /etc/hosts /root/hosts-hard $ ls -li /etc/app.conf # A dangling symlink is not an error to the filesystem, only to the app $ readlink -f /etc/app.conf Finding things, archiving things find-and-tar.sh shell copy # find is a query language: path, test, action # find /etc -type f -name '*.conf' -newermt '-7 days' -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %p\n' | sort # find /var/log -type f -size +50M -exec ls -lh {} + # find /srv -type d -name cache -prune -o -type f -name '*.log' -print # Archives: c=create x=extract t=list f=file z=gzip J=xz j=bzip2 v=verbose # tar -czf /var/tmp/etc-$(date +%F).tar.gz /etc # tar -tzf /var/tmp/etc-2026-10-20.tar.gz | head # tar -xzf /var/tmp/etc-2026-10-20.tar.gz -C /root/restore # Preserve SELinux labels and ownership when archiving a whole tree # tar --selinux -cpzf /var/tmp/srv.tar.gz /srv # restorecon -Rv /srv Exam habit: verify, do not assume After every archive or mount task, list the contents or read the mount table. tar -tzf before you delete the source; findmnt /data after you mount it; ss -tlnp after you start a service. Verification is not extra credit — it is how you find out you scored zero while there is still time to fix it. Documentation: the only offline search engine you get man.sh shell copy $ man 5 passwd # section 5 = file formats $ man 8 mount # section 8 = admin commands $ man -k selinux # same as apropos: search descriptions $ mandb # rebuild the index if man -k finds nothing $ rpm -qd httpd # list docs shipped by a package $ ls /usr/share/doc/httpd/ Useful habit Inside man : / searches forward, n jumps to the next hit, G goes to the end (where EXAMPLES and SEE ALSO live), q quits.
